frameworks.name: Three-Lever Delivery Redesign
frameworks.definition: When founder-dependent delivery creates a supply constraint, reduce delivered hours and scope while repositioning the reduction as an integrity move, then reinvest savings in promised-but-underdelivered services.

frameworks.name: Accessibility Arc
frameworks.definition: Early-stage founders differentiate via founder accessibility (cell phone, rapid response); at scale, accessibility becomes a liability preventing delegation and growth, requiring repositioning of reduced access as earned confidence rather than loss of service.

claims.text: A service business with demand exceeding delivery capacity is supply-constrained, not demand-constrained. Attempting to sell more when supply is the binding constraint wastes marketing effort; the correct lever is delivery redesign or hiring, not increased sales activity.
claims.speaker: Alex Hormozi
conditions: service business with founder-dependent delivery
current capacity fully booked
sales generating more inbound than delivery can handle
claims.mechanism: Without a supply fix, the constraint does not shift, so additional marketing spend produces unserviced leads, wasting capital and damaging reputation through missed deliverables.
bounded_by: Does not apply to demand-constrained businesses (low inbound, empty calendar)
Does not apply to product businesses with unlimited digital delivery

claims.text: A founder's rapid response and constant availability trains customers to expect and demand that behavior, creating an escalating cycle of requests. Changing this pattern requires explicitly retraining customers to a new behavior by consistently not responding outside the new cadence.
claims.speaker: Alex Hormozi
conditions: founder has established pattern of immediate response
customers have learned that quick contact yields quick replies
claims.mechanism: You reward fast requesters with fast answers; they repeat the behavior. To stop the loop, you stop rewarding the behavior (slower response cadence), and eventually customers stop making rapid requests.

claims.text: Early-stage underdog founders differentiate through accessibility—giving direct cell phone access and personal responsiveness where larger competitors appear impersonal. At scale, continued founder accessibility becomes unsustainable and prevents delegation, requiring a narrative reframe: 'I've proven my value; now I can trust my team more,' shifting from accessibility as differentiation to earned confidence.
claims.speaker: Alex Hormozi
conditions: early-stage service business with zero established brand reputation
founder positioning against larger, less personal competitors
founder later approaching capacity or scale challenges
claims.mechanism: In early stage, accessibility is a credible signal of founder commitment when the brand has no proof. At scale, continuing accessibility signals founder insecurity and poor delegation, and blocks growth by preventing systems-based delivery.
bounded_by: Does not apply to product businesses or self-serve models
Does not apply to founder-optional roles (CEO as strategic figurehead rather than day-to-day operator)

claims.text: When reducing delivery scope for clients (fewer hours, fewer calls, fewer personalized touches), do not frame it as a negative reduction ('I'm giving you less'). Instead, position it as a principled integrity move: 'I made a promise I've realized I'm breaking. To stay in integrity with that promise, I must change the delivery model. Here are 17 ways this serves you better.' This shifts client resistance to a question of whether they want to question the founder's integrity.
claims.speaker: Alex Hormozi
conditions: founder-delivered service with existing cohort or client base
founder has made implicit promises about availability or personal involvement
founder is reducing touch (hours, frequency, personalization) to escape founder dependency
claims.mechanism: Framing the change as an integrity move (keeping the promise of the business's mission) reorients the client from defending the old service level to questioning their own integrity if they resist. It also positions the founder as principled rather than backing down.
bounded_by: Requires that the new model still delivers the core promised outcome, not just different delivery method
Requires founder to genuinely believe the reduction improves overall client outcomes, not just founder convenience

claims.text: Founders who are insecure about their value over-deliver—providing far more hours, availability, and support than originally promised—because they worry clients will not perceive sufficient value. This creates a monster by training clients to expect unlimited access, making founder escape impossible without perceived service loss.
claims.speaker: Alex Hormozi
conditions: founder coaching or consulting business (high-touch service)
founder lacks established brand reputation or track record
founder is early-stage and eager to build goodwill in the industry
claims.mechanism: Insecurity → over-promising to reduce perceived risk → clients learn to expect unlimited access → founder burns out and is trapped because changing expectations now appears as a betrayal rather than a correction.

claims.text: The expectations clients have of a founder are set by the founder, not by the clients. If a founder is over-delivering, the founder set those expectations (whether explicitly or through behavior) and the founder must reset them.
claims.speaker: Alex Hormozi
conditions: high-touch founder-delivered service
founder is managing client expectations around availability or scope
claims.mechanism: Responsibility for the expectation lies with the entity that set it. Accepting this shifts the founder from victim ('clients expect too much') to agent ('I set this expectation through my behavior, and I can reset it').

claims.text: A founder experiencing burnout from over-delivery can reframe the delivery change as necessary to preserve their core mission. Instead of 'I'm reducing your support,' the founder says: 'I have a mission to help X number of people. With my current model, I'm out of integrity with that mission—I can't reach that many people. So I'm changing the model to either (a) play smaller and not help that many people, or (b) provide different, equally valuable service so I can help my mission count.' Option (b) reorients from personal service loss to mission fidelity.
claims.speaker: Alex Hormozi
conditions: founder has stated a mission or vision for scale
current delivery model prevents achieving that mission due to founder bandwidth
founder wants to exit founder dependency without appearing to abandon clients
claims.mechanism: Positioning the change as fidelity to a bigger promise (the mission) rather than reduction in a smaller promise (per-client service) reframes the tradeoff. Clients choose between supporting the mission or forcing the founder to play smaller.

claims.text: When implementing a delivery change across multiple existing clients, communicate the change as a universal decision driven by new information, not a custom arrangement for one client. Frame it as: 'This new information has come to my attention. As a result of this new information, these new decisions and actions are happening. Here's why it's great for you. 17 more reasons. And this way I can reinvest in these things you really care about that I haven't been able to do.' This positioning prevents peer pressure from one client influencing others.
claims.speaker: Alex Hormozi
conditions: founder has multiple cohorts or clients with overlapping knowledge of each other
founder is making a uniform delivery change across all clients simultaneously
claims.mechanism: Announcing as a universal decision (not a per-client negotiation) and framing as new information prevents clients from feeling individually wronged or from negotiating around it. It signals that the change is non-negotiable and principle-driven.

claims.text: The founder must actively sell the audience on the delivery change, not expect them to passively accept it. If the founder is internally defensive ('I hate this life, but I'm going to defend it'), the clients will sense the weakness and resist. The founder must be genuinely excited about the new model's benefits and articulate them with conviction.
claims.speaker: Alex Hormozi
conditions: founder is making a delivery or service change to existing clients
founder doubts the change is genuinely better (and is only doing it to escape burnout)
claims.mechanism: Clients sense the founder's internal doubt through tone, word choice, and energy. If the founder is apologetic or defensive, clients assume the change is a loss. If the founder is confident and excited, clients assume it's a genuine improvement.

claims.text: Some clients will leave when a service delivery decreases, even if the new model is genuinely better. This is acceptable because those departing clients came in with old expectations and will be replaced by new clients who pay more and do not carry the legacy expectations of unlimited founder access.
claims.speaker: Alex Hormozi
conditions: founder is reducing delivery scope and repositioning the service
founder has previously trained clients to expect high founder touch
claims.mechanism: Clients with old expectations will feel underserved by the new model; their departure creates space for new clients with different expectations and higher willingness-to-pay, improving unit economics.

claims.text: Handling clients who ask for out-of-cadence contact requires a simple script: route them to a resource, or tell them when the next available slot is on the regular calendar. The key is consistency—do not reward the ask-for-extra-time behavior by saying yes to the request.
claims.speaker: Alex Hormozi
conditions: founder has established a regular cadence of calls or availability
clients periodically ask for additional or out-of-cadence access
claims.mechanism: By consistently not granting out-of-cadence requests and offering a predictable alternative (resource or next scheduled slot), the founder trains clients to stop asking.

claims.text: When a founder is over-delivering on a promise (providing 45 hours of Zoom calls per week when the promise was a 90-minute weekly session), the first step is to reduce delivery to exactly what was promised. The client agreed to the original terms; simply meeting those terms is not a reduction in value, even if it feels like one to the founder.
claims.speaker: Alex Hormozi
conditions: founder is delivering significantly more than originally promised or agreed
founder is conflating over-delivery with expected delivery
claims.mechanism: The client's actual agreement is to the original scope. Meeting that scope is fulfillment, not reduction. Framing it as such helps the founder stop feeling guilty about 'giving less.'

anchors.region: actual current (daily office hours plus cohort sessions plus ad hoc calls)

examples.text: Dog Co. Launch founder is growing a pet-care coaching business from $356k to $1M+ annually. The founder offers cohort-based training (20-25 companies per cohort, twice-yearly launches), plus weekly 90-minute coaching sessions per cohort, plus daily office hours, plus ad hoc calls. The founder is now fully booked and cannot acquire more customers because delivery is maxed out. When asked 'Can you take more customers?' the answer is 'No.' The founder is demand-constrained on the sales side (organic leads from content and speaking) but is actually supply-constrained on the delivery side. Alex Hormozi points out the mismatch: the founder is not demand-constrained; the real lever is delivery redesign (move to evergreen model, compress hours, hire another coach) or staying supply-constrained by choice.

The Dog Co. Launch founder has positioned founder accessibility as a core differentiator early on—'You get my cell phone; you can't get that from the big gyms.' This worked to win the first clients. Now, with six active cohorts and 45 hours per week of Zoom calls, the founder is burned out and the accessibility has become a trap: the cohorts know the founder is available and expect rapid response to questions, creating an endless loop of extra calls. The founder is now so committed to availability that escaping it feels like a betrayal, even though the current model makes scaling impossible.

The founder worries that reducing hours or availability will damage the value clients perceive. Alex Hormozi suggests the opposite: if the founder positions the change as an integrity commitment ('I've realized I'm breaking a promise to help this many dog business owners; to stay in integrity, I'm changing the model'), then the client's choice is whether to question the founder's integrity. By coupling the change to a larger mission (help more dog owners), the founder shifts the story from 'founder is lazy' to 'founder is expanding impact.'

practices.text: When clients ask for out-of-cadence time, respond with a specific routing: 'Here's a resource that can help' or 'The next open slot on my calendar is [date].' Do not say yes to the request, even occasionally—consistency retrains the audience.

Communicate delivery changes as universal, principle-driven decisions: 'New information has come to my attention. As a result, here are these new decisions. Here's why it benefits you. Here are 17 reasons. And this means I can now reinvest in X, which you care about.' Avoid framing as a custom negotiation.

When repositioning a delivery reduction, genuinely believe it improves client outcomes or the clients will sense the founder's doubt. If the founder is only doing it to escape burnout, sell the audience on the real benefits rather than defending the change defensively.

Separate the message about current over-delivery: 'You agreed to X. I'm currently giving you X + Y. I'm going to give you X, which is what you agreed to.' This reframes the reduction from 'losing value' to 'normalizing to contract.'
